chunks: Ibn Muskan narrated from Isa ibn Abi Mansur, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a group of people who buy Herawi, Karawi, Marwazi, or Quhi bundles of clothes. A man among them purchases ten garments, stipulating a condition that each garment is worth five dirhams, or less, or more. He said: 'I do not like this type of sale. What if he does not find any choice among them except five garments, and the rest are all the same?' Then Isma'il, his son, said to him: 'They have stipulated that he must take ten garments from them.' He repeatedly responded: 'He has only stipulated with them to take the best among them. What if he only finds five that are suitable, and the rest are all the same?' Then he said: 'I do not like this type of sale.'

key_terms.الْجِرَاب: A bundle or sack of goods, specifically clothes in this context
key_terms.خِيَار: Choice or option; the right to select the best from a group
key_terms.دَرَاهِم: Dirhams, a unit of currency used in the transaction
key_terms.سَوَاء: Equal or the same, referring to the uniform quality of the remaining items

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on buying a bundle of goods with a condition to select only the best items while being forced to take the rest?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (as) critiques the 'bundle sale' (bay' al-jirab) of Herat or Marv carpets, where a buyer selects a few premium items but is forced to accept the remainder regardless of quality, effectively nullifying the right of option (khiyar) for the majority. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on preventing hidden defects (gharar) and ensuring equitable exchange, warning against commercial practices that disguise unfairness through contractual stipulations. The Imam’s repeated expression of dislike underscores the principle that a condition must be practically meaningful to be valid in Islamic trade.
